q: Which class of biomolecule stores and passes on genetic information?
e: DNA and RNA are nucleic acids made of nucleotides.

q: Enzymes belong to which class of biomolecules?
e: Enzymes are proteins folded into specific shapes.

q: Why do phospholipids form a double layer in a cell membrane?
o: Both ends of the molecule repel water
They are made of amino acids that bond tightly
Their heads are attracted to water and their tails avoid water
They store genetic information in the layer
e: The hydrophilic heads face the watery surroundings and the hydrophobic tails face inward.

q: What are the building blocks (monomers) of proteins?
e: Amino acids join in chains to make proteins.

q: Starch and cellulose are examples of which biomolecule class?
e: They are long chains of sugar units.

q: Which biomolecules are the best long-term energy storage in animals?
e: Fats store more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

q: Which structure do bacterial cells lack?
e: Prokaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleoid region without a membrane.

q: Which of these organisms is made of eukaryotic cells?
o: a bacterium that lives in soil
an archaeon from a hot spring
e: Fungi are eukaryotes, while bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.

q: Which structure do both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have?
e: All cells make proteins at ribosomes.

q: According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria originated from what?
o: a part of the nucleus that pinched off
small prokaryotes engulfed by a larger cell
e: Evidence includes their own circular DNA and double membranes.

q: How is the DNA of a typical bacterium organized?
o: as DNA packed in the mitochondria
as RNA inside a protein coat
as a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm
as many linear chromosomes inside a nucleus
e: Prokaryotic DNA is circular and lies in the nucleoid.

q: What is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane called?
e: Water moves toward the side with more dissolved solute.

q: In simple diffusion, molecules move in which direction?
o: from high concentration to low concentration
from low concentration to high concentration
e: Diffusion follows the concentration gradient and needs no energy.

q: What does active transport require that passive transport does not?
e: It moves substances against their gradient.

q: A red blood cell is placed in distilled water. What most likely happens?
e: Water rushes into the cell because the outside has fewer solutes.

q: How does facilitated diffusion move a molecule across a membrane?
o: by pumping it against its gradient with ATP
by engulfing it in a vesicle
through a carrier or channel protein without using energy
e: The molecule still moves down its gradient.

q: Why are viruses not considered cells?
o: They lack organelles and cannot reproduce without a host
They are too large to be seen
They have a nucleus but no membrane
e: Viruses are genetic material in a protein coat.

q: What is the protein coat of a virus called?
e: The capsid protects the viral genetic material.

q: Why don't antibiotics treat influenza?
o: Antibiotics target bacteria, and viruses are not bacteria
e: Viruses lack the structures that antibiotics attack.

q: A virus enters a host cell and uses it to make more viruses. This is the virus's way of doing what?
e: Viruses hijack the host's machinery to reproduce.

q: During which part of the cell cycle is DNA copied?
e: The S (synthesis) phase replicates the chromosomes.

q: Mitosis produces how many cells, and how do they compare to the parent cell?
o: one large cell with two nuclei
two cells genetically identical to the parent
two cells genetically different from each other
four cells with half the chromosomes
e: Mitosis makes identical diploid daughter cells.

q: What is the correct order of the stages of mitosis?
e: PMAT.

q: In which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up along the center of the cell?
e: The spindle fibers align them at the equator.

q: Which part of the cell cycle takes up most of the time for a typical dividing cell?
e: Cells grow and copy DNA during interphase.

q: What is cell differentiation?
o: the breakdown of a cell by enzymes
the process by which cells become specialized in structure and function
the movement of water across membranes
the process by which a cell copies its DNA
e: Different genes are switched on in different cell types.

q: A muscle cell and a nerve cell in the same person differ mainly because of what?
o: the number of chromosomes they have
which genes are expressed in each
e: Both contain the same DNA but use different parts of it.

q: What is special about stem cells?
o: They are unspecialized and can differentiate into other cell types
e: Stem cells can develop into specialized cells.

q: Which is an example of an environmental factor that can influence cell differentiation?
o: the age of the parent's cells
the color of the organism's eyes
the number of ribosomes in the cell
e: Signals around a developing cell help turn genes on or off.

q: Cancer is best described as what?
o: uncontrolled cell division caused by a failure in cell cycle control
the death of too many cells
the failure of cells to take in nutrients
e: Damaged control genes allow cells to keep dividing.

q: What is the role of tumor suppressor genes?
o: They slow cell division and repair DNA errors
They make cells unable to die
e: When they are damaged, the cell loses a brake on division.

q: Which is an example of a carcinogen?
e: Carcinogens cause DNA mutations that can lead to cancer.

q: What makes a tumor malignant?
o: its cells can invade other tissues and spread
it is made of fat cells
e: Spreading to other body parts is called metastasis.

q: What three parts make up a DNA nucleotide?
o: a sugar, an enzyme and water
a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen base
a phosphate, a protein and a fatty acid
an amino acid, a sugar and a lipid
e: Nucleotides are the units of DNA.

q: In DNA, adenine pairs with which base?
e: A pairs with T and C pairs with G.

q: What part of DNA contains the code that determines traits?
o: the order of its nitrogen bases
e: The base sequence is read in groups of three to specify amino acids.

q: One strand of DNA reads AATGC. What is the complementary strand?
e: A↔T and C↔G.

q: What is the shape of a DNA molecule?
e: Two strands twist around each other.

q: Where does transcription occur in a eukaryotic cell?
e: DNA is copied into mRNA inside the nucleus.

q: Where does translation occur?
e: Ribosomes read mRNA to build a protein.

q: Which base does RNA use instead of thymine?
e: RNA contains A, U, C and G.

q: What is a codon?
o: a group of three mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid
e: The ribosome reads mRNA one codon at a time.

q: What does a tRNA molecule do?
o: it stores the genetic code in the nucleus
it brings the matching amino acid to the ribosome
e: Its anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon.

q: A DNA template strand reads TAC GGT. What is the mRNA made from it?
e: T→A, A→U, C→G and G→C.

q: What is a point mutation?
o: a change in a single nucleotide of DNA
a change in the cell membrane
a copy of the whole genome
the loss of an entire chromosome
e: One base is replaced, added or removed.

q: Why is a frameshift mutation usually more harmful than a substitution?
o: It shifts the reading frame and changes every codon after it
It only affects the first codon
e: An insertion or deletion alters all the following codons.

q: A mutation that does not change the amino acid sequence is called what?
e: Several codons can code for the same amino acid.

q: A mutation in a body (somatic) cell, such as a skin cell, is passed on to offspring how?
o: It is passed on to every cell in the offspring
It is passed on only to sons
e: Only mutations in gametes can be inherited.

q: What does PCR do?
o: makes many copies of a DNA segment
e: Polymerase chain reaction amplifies DNA.

q: What does gel electrophoresis separate?
e: An electric current pulls DNA through a gel.

q: In gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragments travel farthest?
o: the fragments with the most guanine only
e: Small pieces move more easily through the gel.

q: Putting the human insulin gene into bacteria so they make insulin is an example of what?
e: DNA from one species is inserted into another.

q: What do restriction enzymes do?
o: cut DNA at specific base sequences
e: They are used to cut DNA for cloning.

q: What does meiosis produce from one diploid cell?
e: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and makes gametes.

q: During which stage of meiosis does crossing-over occur?
e: Homologous chromosomes swap segments while paired.

q: What is independent assortment?
o: the pairing of A with T
the random way homologous pairs line up and separate
e: It creates many different combinations of chromosomes in gametes.

q: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a human sperm cell have?
e: Meiosis reduces the number by half.

q: Failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis is called what?
e: It can lead to conditions such as Down syndrome.

q: In a cross of two heterozygous parents (Tt × Tt), what fraction of offspring are expected to be tt?
e: The Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

q: A heterozygous parent (Tt) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (tt). What fraction of offspring are expected to be tt?
e: Half of the offspring get t from the heterozygote.

q: A cross of two parents that are both RrYy (two traits) gives which phenotype ratio when each trait shows complete dominance?
e: This is the classic dihybrid ratio.

q: A red snapdragon is crossed with a white snapdragon and all offspring are pink. This is an example of what?
e: The heterozygote shows a blend.

q: A person with type AB blood shows both A and B traits. This is an example of what?
e: Both alleles are fully expressed.

q: Why are X-linked recessive disorders more common in males?
o: The Y chromosome carries the allele
Males have only one X chromosome, so one recessive allele is expressed
e: A single recessive allele on the X shows up in XY individuals.

q: The arm of a human and the wing of a bat have similar bone structures. What are these called?
e: They suggest a common ancestor.

q: What do the fossils in layers of rock show about life on Earth?
o: how organisms have changed over time
that all organisms appeared at once
e: The fossil record records past life in order.

q: Pelvic bones in a whale are very small and have no clear use. What type of structure are they?
e: They are remnants from ancestors that walked on land.

q: Two species share a very high percentage of DNA. What does that suggest?
o: they live in the same habitat
they share a recent common ancestor
e: More similar DNA suggests closer relation.

q: Marsupials are found mostly in Australia and nearby islands. How does biogeography explain this?
o: Related groups spread and diversified after the continents separated
Australia has no predators for them
e: Geographic isolation led to unique lineages.

q: Which idea says that species change slowly and steadily over long periods?
e: Small changes accumulate over time.

q: Which idea says that long periods of little change are interrupted by short bursts of rapid change?
e: The fossil record often shows such bursts.

q: What is stasis in the fossil record?
o: a long period with little or no change in a species
e: The species stays nearly the same.

q: Which can evolve over generations?
o: a single cell during its life
a single gene during an individual's life
e: Allele frequencies change in populations.

q: Soot darkens tree bark, and dark peppered moths become more common than light ones. What explains this?
o: Light moths migrated away on their own
Dark moths were better hidden and survived more often
Dark moths were created by the soot
e: Natural selection favors traits that help survival.

q: What does fitness mean in biology?
o: how well an organism survives and reproduces
e: Fitness is reproductive success.

q: Why can't an individual organism evolve through natural selection?
o: natural selection acts on DNA only
its genes stay the same during its life, so selection changes the population
e: Allele frequencies change across generations.

q: Which is NOT required for natural selection?
o: traits acquired during an organism's life being passed on
e: Only inherited variation is acted on.

q: Why do some bacteria become resistant to antibiotics over time?
o: Antibiotics change the bacteria's DNA on purpose
Resistant bacteria survive treatment and reproduce more
e: Selection favors the resistant variants.

q: What does it mean that populations have the potential to overproduce?
o: they produce exactly the number that survive
they make more offspring than the environment can support
e: That leads to competition.

q: What is an adaptation?
o: an inherited trait that improves survival and reproduction in an environment
e: Adaptations arise through natural selection.

q: Which event can lead to the formation of a new species?
e: Isolated populations diverge.

q: By the biological species concept, a species is a group that can do what?
e: Reproductive isolation defines separate species.

q: A river splits a squirrel population, and over time the two groups can no longer mate. What is this an example of?
e: Isolation and different selection lead to new species.

q: What is adaptive radiation?
o: the movement of animals between populations
rapid diversification of one ancestral species into many forms for different niches
e: Darwin's finches are an example.

q: What is genetic drift?
o: random changes in allele frequencies, especially in small populations
changes caused by the environment selecting traits
e: Chance events change allele frequencies.

q: What is gene flow?
o: the movement of alleles between populations through migration
e: Migrants carry alleles into new populations.

q: A disease kills most of a population, leaving a few survivors with a limited set of alleles. What is this called?
e: Genetic variation drops after a sharp population decline.

q: What is the ultimate source of new alleles in a population?
e: Mutations create new versions of genes.

q: A few individuals colonize a new island, and their small gene pool differs from the original. What is this called?
e: A small starting group may not represent the whole population.

q: What are the reactants of photosynthesis?
e: Light energy is also needed.

q: What are the products of photosynthesis?
e: Plants make sugar and release O₂.

q: Where does most cellular respiration take place in a eukaryotic cell?
e: Mitochondria produce most of a cell's ATP.

q: What are the products of aerobic cellular respiration?
e: Glucose is broken down with oxygen.

q: A student says that matter is lost during cellular respiration. What is the correct idea?
o: atoms are rearranged into new molecules, so matter is conserved
e: Conservation of matter holds in all chemical reactions.

q: Which pigment in chloroplasts captures light for photosynthesis?
e: Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light.

q: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
o: by being used up in the reaction
by adding heat to the reaction
e: Enzymes are catalysts and are not consumed.

q: Where does the substrate bind on an enzyme?
e: Its shape fits the substrate.

q: Why does an enzyme stop working at very high temperature?
o: it floats away from the cell
its shape changes (denatures), so the active site no longer fits
e: Denaturation destroys the active site shape.

q: Pepsin works best in the acidic stomach. What does this show?
e: Different enzymes work best at different pH values.

q: Which two systems mainly regulate the body's activities through signals?
e: Neurons use electrical signals and glands use hormones.

q: After nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, which system carries them to body cells?
e: Blood transports absorbed nutrients.

q: What is the role of villi in the small intestine?
e: Folds and projections increase absorption.

q: Blood sugar rises after a meal, and the pancreas releases insulin, which lowers it. This is an example of what?
e: The response reverses the change.

q: Which plant tissue carries water and minerals upward from the roots?
e: Xylem moves water upward.

q: Which plant tissue carries sugars made in the leaves to other parts?
e: Phloem transports sugar in sap.

q: What do stomata do?
o: allow gas exchange and water vapor loss
e: Guard cells open and close them.

q: Phototropism is a plant's growth response to what?
e: Stems bend toward light.

q: Which plant hormone helps cause stems to bend toward light?
e: Auxin builds up on the shaded side and lengthens those cells.

q: Bees collect nectar from flowers while pollinating them. This is an example of what?
e: Both species benefit.

q: A tapeworm lives in the intestines of a dog and takes nutrients, harming it. This is an example of what?
e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

q: Birds build nests in a tree, which benefits the birds but does not affect the tree. This is an example of what?
e: One species benefits and the other is unaffected.

q: Two species of plants compete for the same limited sunlight. This is an example of what?
e: They use the same limited resource.

q: A lynx hunts snowshoe hares. This relationship is an example of what?
e: The predator kills and eats the prey.

q: About how much energy is passed from one trophic level to the next?
e: Most energy is lost as heat.

q: Which organisms form the base of most food chains?
e: Producers capture energy from sunlight.

q: If the top predator in a food web is removed, what might happen to the herbivore population?
o: it will stay exactly the same
it may grow and overgraze the producers
e: Predators limit prey populations.

q: Which statement about energy and matter in an ecosystem is true?
o: energy flows in one direction while matter is recycled
matter flows one way while energy is recycled
e: Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat.

q: What role do decomposers play in an ecosystem?
o: break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil
e: They recycle nutrients.

q: What do nitrogen-fixing bacteria do?
o: convert nitrogen gas into forms plants can use
e: They make ammonia from atmospheric N₂.

q: Burning fossil fuels affects the carbon cycle in what way?
o: it removes carbon from the air
it releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
e: Stored carbon is released as CO₂.

q: What process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere into living things?
e: Plants convert CO₂ into sugars.

q: Fertilizer runoff reaches a lake and causes a large algae bloom. What problem may follow?
o: oxygen levels drop and aquatic life dies
e: Decomposing algae use up oxygen.

q: Clearing large forests affects the carbon cycle how?
o: less carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants
e: Fewer plants mean less photosynthesis.

q: What is the leading cause of biodiversity loss?
e: Species lose the places where they live.

q: How can an invasive species harm an ecosystem?
o: it can outcompete native species for resources
e: Invasive species often have no natural predators.

q: Why are ecosystems with high biodiversity often more stable?
o: if one species declines, others can fill its role
e: Many species provide redundancy.

q: What is a keystone species?
o: a species with a large effect on its ecosystem relative to its numbers
e: Removing it can change the whole community.
